paper_metadata.title: Quantum Machine Learning Technique for Insurance Claim Fraud Detection with Quantum Feature Selection

summary: The paper evaluates a QSVM with a ZZ feature map for insurance claim fraud detection using a proprietary dataset with 15 features. Reported accuracies are 97.3% (KNN), 99.0% (classical SVM), and 98.3% (QSVM), with the experiments performed in simulation rather than on real quantum hardware.

experiments.description: Insurance claim fraud detection using QSVM with ZZ feature map on IBM Quantum/Qiskit, compared against classical KNN and SVM baselines.

problem_formulation.encoding_details: Classical fraud-detection features are mapped into a quantum feature space via a ZZ feature map; the paper does not specify a binary-variable QUBO encoding.
problem_formulation.objective_function: Binary classification of insurance claims into fraudulent or non-fraudulent classes using a quantum kernel-based SVM.

problem_instance.description: Home insurance claim fraud detection on a real claims-payment dataset with historical suspicious activity reporting filings.

dataset_specification.description: 15 parameters with weighted scores; personally identifiable information scrubbed; includes credit score, payment default history, outstanding debts, property age, occupancy duration, claims history, loss timing flags, authority notification/report availability.

problem_instance.data_preprocessing_details: Normalize and scale the data; apply feature selection to reduce dimensionality; use quantum feature selection / engineered features; the paper does not specify train-test split.
problem_instance.evaluation_methodology: Comparative evaluation against classical KNN and SVM using accuracy; also mentions recall and false positive rate, but only accuracy values are reported in the provided text.

implementation_details.classical_solver: Qiskit quantum kernel / QSVM; classical baselines KNN and SVM

speedup_claims.caveats: The paper reports comparable performance between classical and quantum methods, but does not claim or demonstrate a speedup.

complexity_analysis.quantum_complexity: Not reported for this paper; background cites QSVM/kernel methods generally.

advantage_assessment.crossover_size: Not reported; dataset size unspecified and experiment performed only on a small simulated instance.
advantage_assessment.resources_for_advantage: Not analyzed in the paper. Achieving advantage would require substantially larger feature maps, larger datasets, and fault‑tolerant quantum hardware capable of large kernel evaluations.
limiting_factors: Classical SVM baseline achieves higher accuracy (99.0%) than QSVM (98.3%).
Experiments performed only on simulation, not real quantum hardware.
Dataset size and scaling behavior not reported.
No complexity analysis or runtime comparison.
Kernel evaluation requires classical data loading into quantum feature maps.

notes: 3 qubits and depth=1 are taken from the ZZ feature map figure/caption context ('feature = 3, depth = 1').
Hardware is reported as IBM Quantum processors through Qiskit, but no specific device name is given.
The paper reports accuracy for KNN, SVM, and QSVM; classical methods are recorded as baselines, not separate experiments.
No explicit gate counts, shots, optimizer, or transpilation details are provided.
Table 2 shows SVM accuracy 99.0%, QSVM accuracy 98.3%, so the classical baseline outperforms the quantum method.
Authors do not claim a computational speedup or quantum advantage; they state performance is comparable and exploratory.
